title: DC-area forecast: Welcome to Sizzle-tember, with hot 90s and storm chances
contentHtml:
Always a human at the helm: Updated around-the-clock by Capital Weather meteorologists.

Happening now: A partly to mostly sunny morning with temperatures quickly climbing from the 70s into the 80s. Highs reach the mid- to upper 90s this afternoon with moderate to high humidity. A few late-day storms are possible.

What’s next? More heat and humidity Wednesday and Thursday, although a nearby cool front lowers temperatures a bit in some areas and triggers storms, especially Wednesday afternoon and evening. We start to cool down Friday before more comfortable temperatures and lower humidity arrive for the weekend.

Today’s daily digit — 2/10: September starts with a failing back-to-school grade thanks to high heat and humidity, plus the chance of storms. | 🤚 Your call?
The digit is a somewhat subjective rating of the day’s weather, on a 0-to-10 scale.

Forecast in detail

Today (Tuesday): Partly sunny this morning as temperatures climb through the muggy 80s, with afternoon highs in the mid-90s to even upper 90s in a few spots. With dew points near 70, heat indexes peak around 100 to 105. Winds are from the west at 5 to 10 mph.

An isolated shower or thunderstorm becomes possible by afternoon into early evening, especially across the northern half of the area. Heavy downpours and gusty winds are possible. Confidence: Medium-High

Tonight: An evening shower or thunderstorm is possible; otherwise, expect partly cloudy skies and muggy lows from the low 70s in our cooler areas to the mid- to upper 70s downtown. Winds are from the west at about 5 mph. Confidence: Medium-High

Hourly Forecast | Pollen, Air & UV

Tomorrow (Wednesday): Hump day may see some bumps as strong heat clashes with a cool front arriving from the northeast. This could produce some large temperature differences over relatively short distances.

For DC and points south, we should see partly to mostly sunny skies with highs in the mid-90s and heat indexes topping 100. Areas to the north, from Frederick to Baltimore, could see partly to mostly cloudy skies with highs in the upper 80s to low 90s. Potentially strong to severe thunderstorms could erupt during the afternoon and evening, with threats of heavy rain and damaging wind gusts. Confidence: Low-Medium

Tomorrow night: After evening storm chances, the overnight should turn partly cloudy and remain muggy, with lows in the 70s. Confidence: Medium

A look ahead

Thursday should fire up another round of 90s across the area. Highs range from the lower 90s north to the upper 90s south amid partly to mostly sunny skies. Humidity remains on the moderate to high side. Scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible during the afternoon and evening, followed by mostly cloudy skies Thursday night and muggy lows in the 70s. Confidence: Medium

The heat starts to back off a bit Friday, but we should still see highs in the low 90s, and even mid-90s toward Fredericksburg, under partly to mostly sunny skies. Lingering humidity, with dew points near 70, helps afternoon and evening thunderstorms flare up. Temperatures start to cool Friday night under partly cloudy skies, with lows from the mid-60s to near 70. Confidence: Medium

The weekend brings gradual relief from the heat. Highs reach the mid- to upper 80s Saturday, when a shower or storm remains possible. Sunday looks very nice with sunny skies, highs in the upper 70s to low 80s and lower humidity. Sunday night should be pleasant, with lows in the 60s and even some upper 50s possible in our cooler suburbs. Confidence: Medium

Labor Day and the rest of next week feature fairly calm conditions with gradually rising temperatures. Highs should climb from the low 80s early in the week to the mid-80s by midweek, with a shot at upper 80s to low 90s by Thursday and Friday, along with a slight chance of late-day thunderstorms.

DC weather history for September 1

Violent weather defines this date, from a thunderstorm-drenched Civil War battle in 1862 to record rains, hurricane remnants, and destructive tornadoes in multiple years.
